doc.title: Daryl Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2024

title: What makes her drop a musician from her call list; Boots Malison
summary: Asked about behavior that would move someone down her list, she says it rarely happens and describes using Boots Malison and Jay Leonhart.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Yeah. I want to wrap up with a question that might be worthwhile for up-and-coming musicians. Most of us have lists of players to call when we get a gig and we have to
assemble a group. And what kind of behavior — either musical or otherwise — would make you move someone down your list as opposed to up your list?

That’s an interesting question. Rarely would it happen. Maybe something that was treasonous like I mean it hasn’t happened, but if someone was trying to hustle a gig, I don’t know. If someone got terribly drunk and passed out or did something I might have to be. I don’t know. Huh.

Well now actually — or just someone who was clearly not — not getting my groove and not, but you know, then again I’m not — particularly at this time of life I’m not, you know, I’m not so easily destined to be hiring somebody that I don’t know. I might sometime, and I should because it’s always nice to play with other people. But you want your comfort level. And sometimes things go wrong even with them and you get, you know like why did he do that to me. And why did he blah-blah-blah. But still, you know, you’re like a dysfunctional family. I have, I have different people that I like to use to emphasize different things. Like I have Boots Malison who has five strings, he remembers everything I played in 1980, he’s got a beautiful sound, he’s quick, he can read everything. And yet my first bass player when I came to New York was Jay Leonhart.
